# Business-Model Transition to Subscription — First Draft for Comment

**Prepared for the CEO, CFO, CRO, Chief Product Officer and Chief Customer Officer, with the Audit Committee chair and the Board's lead independent director in attendance.**
*Circulated for comment before any decision is sought. Figures marked "illustrative" are placeholders for the Week 8 model; the offer architecture, the entitlement charter, the compensation mechanics, the tripwires and the decision requests are not placeholders, and are put forward for approval.*

---

## 0. Executive summary

**The situation, stated plainly and without attribution of fault.** Our revenue is lumpy because our model makes it lumpy, and the market discounts what it cannot forecast. Leadership wants recurring revenue. The modelling says we cannot get there without a multi-year trough. The field is paid on the very deals we intend to stop selling. The installed base believes — accurately — that it bought something perpetual. And the one nearby precedent we have lost a fifth of its base moving quickly.

Four constituencies each hold an internally coherent position: the field is right that its economics break; the CFO is right that the trough is real; customers are right that they own what they bought; Product is right that we cannot fund a cloud platform out of upgrade cycles. All four being right is precisely why no single function can resolve this.

**The central finding we expect the diagnostic to confirm.** The trough and the entitlement problem have almost nothing to do with each other, and are routinely confused:

- **The trough is a timing artefact of *new* business** — a licence recognised on delivery becomes an annual fee recognised ratably — compounded by the disappearance of paid-upgrade revenue.
- **Converting the installed base is revenue-*accretive*, not dilutive**, provided the subscription price sits meaningfully above current maintenance. The obstacle there is trust, not arithmetic.

The failure mode — and, we suspect, our competitor's — is **paying for the second problem with discounts that permanently deepen the first.**

**The organising principle we would propose:** *ARR list price is sacred; everything around it is fair game.* Every migration incentive must pass one test: *does this concession cost us cash once, or revenue forever?* Duration, scope, credits, terms, rights and patience are one-time currencies. A discount to the recurring rate is a permanent tax on the outcome we are buying.

**A second principle, for the capital-markets half of the plan:** *we will be judged on the shape of the trough we predicted, far more than on the depth of the trough we hit.* Which argues for publishing the curve in advance and then hitting waypoints, rather than guiding conservatively and explaining quarterly.

**The commitment we would ask colleagues to consider, in three deliberate stages:**

| | Posture | Earned by | Timing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1 — Coexistence** | Subscription is the default quote; perpetual remains available, unmoved in price | Pilot conversion economics in two segments; comp plan shadow-run | Q1–Q2 |
| **Stage 2 — Divergence** | New capability ships subscription-only; perpetual price steps up on a published schedule | Conversion ratio ≥ 2.2×, base churn within tripwire | Q3 – Yr 2 |
| **Stage 3 — Legacy** | Perpetual maintained but not sold to new logos | ARR crossover trajectory on plan | Yr 3+ |

There will be understandable pressure to compress this. It may be worth agreeing early that **no customer is ever forced to move, and every customer is eventually paid to** — and that the second half of that sentence does the work.

**Illustrative shape of the transition (to be replaced by the Week 8 model; base year revenue $240M, ARR $70M):**

| | Yr 0 | Yr 1 | Yr 2 | Yr 3 | Yr 4 | Yr 5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Total revenue ($M) | 240 | 205 | **186** | 199 | 232 | 272 |
| vs. base | — | −15% | **−22%** | −17% | −3% | +13% |
| ARR ($M) | 70 | 105 | 155 | 205 | 250 | 300 |
| Subscription mix | 0% | 15% | 38% | 60% | 78% | 90% |
| FCF ($M) | 40 | 18 | **8** | 25 | 45 | 60 |

Trough depth ≈ 22%; trough quarter ≈ Q3 Yr 2; revenue crossover ≈ Yr 4; cumulative FCF shortfall against baseline ≈ **$95M** over three years, which sets the liquidity requirement and, we would suggest, the true size of the ask.

**The honest framing, which we would rather state ourselves than have an analyst state for us:** on five-year cumulative rev

# Lead Time Reduction Plan — Second Draft

**Prepared for review by the Managing Director and the three functional leaders (Production, Quality, Sales), with Engineering and Procurement in attendance.**
*Circulated for comment before any decision is sought. Numbers marked "illustrative" are placeholders to be replaced by the Week 6 business case; the governance, ownership and decision requests are not placeholders and are put forward for approval.*

---

## 0. Executive summary

**The situation, stated plainly but without attribution of fault.** We quote 14 weeks; our fastest competitor quotes 6; Sales reports losing roughly one deal in three on delivery. A previous attempt to compress the schedule produced a warranty spike that took two years to recover from. The three functions currently hold three different, internally coherent explanations of where the time goes. All three may well be partly right, which is precisely why no single function can resolve it.

**The central finding we expect the diagnostic to confirm.** In a build of this type, of a 14-week (≈70 working-day) quoted lead time, we estimate around **55 working days are waiting** — material queues, gate dwell, rework loops, administrative serialisation, and quote padding — and roughly **15 days are genuine value-adding work, of which the certified inspections themselves are about one day.** The prior compression episode, as best we can reconstruct it, compressed the 15 rather than the 55. That is the difference this plan turns on.

**The organising principle.** *Touch time is treated as sacred; queue time is fair game.* Every intervention must pass the test: *does this change what we inspect, or only when and how quickly the part reaches the inspector?* Where an intervention does change a control — and two of them do — it is presented openly as a **substitution of controls with equivalence evidence**, not as a free saving.

**The commitment we would ask colleagues to consider, in two deliberate stages:**

| | Quoted lead time (configure-to-order lane) | Earned by | Target date |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1** | **7 calendar weeks** (35 working days) | Flow, material, gate-dwell and rework improvements demonstrated in a pilot lane | Month 8 |
| **Stage 2** | **6 calendar weeks** (30 working days) | Demonstrated reduction in schedule variance permitting a smaller quote buffer | Month 14–16 |

Sales will understandably prefer to sell the endpoint immediately. It may be worth agreeing together that a **reliable 7 beats an optimistic 6**, and that the buffer is the last thing we spend, not the first.

**Illustrative investment ask (order of magnitude; to be firmed by Week 6):**

| Item | Year-1 cost | Working capital | Note |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Certified sub-assembly stock | — | £2.0–3.0M net | Gross £2.8–4.2M, reduced by aftermarket alignment (§10) |
| Inspection & metrology capacity (3 inspectors + 1 metrology technician) | £0.32M/yr | — | Recruitment lead time 3–6 months; interim third-party source inspection |
| Configurator (quote-to-BOM) | £0.25–0.45M | — | 6–9 months to live; **not** a quick win |
| eQMS / concurrent certification records | £0.30–0.60M | — | 9–12 months; registrar review required |
| In-process metrology, CMM programming, data capture | £0.40–0.70M | — | Phased by gate |
| MRP/ATP configuration | £0.12M | — | |
| Programme resource (lead + analyst) | £0.25M/yr | — | |
| **Total** | **£1.6–2.4M** | **£2.0–3.0M** | |

**Illustrative return.** On assumptions to be validated in Week 2 (200 qualified opportunities/yr, ~£180k average order value, ~37 losses/yr attributed to delivery, recovery of half of those falling in the fast lanes), incremental bookings of **£3.0–3.6M/yr** at ~30% contribution, plus **£0.4–0.7M/yr** of avoided rework, scrap and expedite cost, and a reduction in warranty exposure that we would not attempt to monetise in front of this audience. Indicative payback **20–26 months** including working capital. *If the Week 2 win/loss validation does not support the revenue figure, the correct recommendation is to fund only the near-zero-cost workstreams and stop.*

**Ownership — the change we believe matters most.** Today, end-to-end lead time is nobody's single measure, and each function is being asked to optimise something that makes it worse. We propose a named **Flow Owner** accountable for quoted lead time end-to-end, a weekly **Flow Council**, and a shared scorecard across all three leaders. Details in §2.

**Decisions requested (also listed in §14):** appoint sponsor and Flow Owner (Week 0); authorise the diagnostic and the certification enquiry (Week 0); approve the shared scorecard (Week 4); approve capital and working capital (Week 8, on the business case); approve Stage 1 quoting (Month 8, on pilot evidence).

---

## 1. How we would suggest this plan is taken forward

A plan of this kind will not succeed by being circulated and approved. Before the first Flow Council, we would propose:

1. **Separate one-to-one conversations** with the Production, Quality, Sales, Engineering and Procurement leaders, in seniority order, so that each has the opportunity to shape the parts touching their area *before* anything is presented collectively. Disagreements are far easier to accommodate at that stage than in a room.
2. **A short, sponsor-signed statement on the prior episode** — that it is now understood as a failure of system design under commercial pressure, not of individual judgement; and that **exercising quality stop authority will carry no career consequence, ever, and requires no escalation.** This costs nothing and, in our view, is the precondition for Quality's genuine (rather than formal) participation.
3. **A shared statement of what is not on the table**, agreed in advance: acceptance criteria, gate content, and stop authority. Once colleagues are confident these are secure, a great deal becomes discussable that is currently not.
4. **Publication of every diagnostic finding**, including those unflattering to whichever function commissioned the work, and including any that reflect on management scheduling practice.

The tone throughout should be that all three functions are currently doing what their measures ask of them. The measures are the problem we can change.

---

## 2. Governance, ownership and the alignment question

### 2.1 Structure

| Role | Holder (by position) | Accountability |
|---|---|---|
| **Executive sponsor** | Managing Director | Removes cross-functional deadlocks; signs the no-retribution statement; owns the funding case |
| **Flow Owner** (new, single point of accountability) | Director of Order Fulfilment (or equivalent senior appointment) | **Quoted and actual end-to-end lead time.** Convenes the Council; owns the plan; has release authority over the single sequence (§7D) |
| **Flow Council** | Flow Owner (chair), Production Manager, Quality Director, Sales Director, Engineering Manager, Procurement Manager | Weekly, 60 minutes, standing agenda: tripwire status, gate dwell, kit completeness, lane mix, escalations |
| **Escalation path** | Council → sponsor | Any item unresolved in Council is escalated with a written position from each function and **decided by the sponsor within 48 hours**. Silence is not consent; unresolved items do not simply age |
| **Quality Director** | — | Retains unconditional veto on anything touching gate content, sampling, or certification. This veto is not subject to Council majority |

Placing an explicit veto with Quality is deliberate. It is the mechanism by which speed becomes safe to pursue, and it should be stated in writing rather than assumed.

### 2.2 Shared scorecard — the substantive change

We would propose adding the following to **all three** functional leaders' scorecards, at equal weight, from the next review cycle:

| Measure | Definition |
|---|---|
| **OTIF against the *first* promised date** | Not the revised date. Re-promising is the mechanism by which delay currently becomes invisible |
| **Escape rate** | Defects found downstream of the gate that should have caught them |
| **Quoted-lead-time attainment** | Actual vs. quoted, by lane |

And, more delicately, we would suggest the sponsor consider retiring or neutralising three measures that are, we believe, generating the present friction rather than any individual doing so:

- **Production's utilisation / absorption target.** This measure rewards loading WIP onto the floor, and will quietly resist the WIP cap in §7D. It cannot survive alongside this plan. Suggested replacement: schedule adherence and throughput at the constraint.
- **Quality's inspections-completed throughput measure.** It discourages the very thing we need — inspectors idle at a gate, waiting, so that nothing else waits for them.
- **Sales' commission timing on booked orders regardless of deliverability.** Suggested adjustment: a portion of commission contingent on delivery to the first promised date, which aligns Sales with the lane discipline in §9.

We recognise these are compensation-adjacent matters requiring HR involvement and the sponsor's authority. We would not propose them lightly, but the arithmetic does not work without them.

---

## 3. Diagnostic: Weeks 0–4 (and what to do when the data does not exist)

### 3.1 Instruments

| Instrument | Method | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
| Order-level time ladder | Last 60–100 shipped orders: timestamp every state change from order receipt to ship | Programme analyst | Wk 3 |
| Touch-time vs. elapsed-time ratio | Standard hours ÷ elapsed working hours | Production Manager | Wk 3 |
| **Gate dwell decomposition** | Per gate: *waiting for inspector / inspection / waiting for sign-off / waiting for rework / re-inspection* | Quality Director | Wk 4 |
| Rework loop census | Every NCR: detected where, caused where, days lost, supplier or internal | Quality Director | Wk 4 |
| Material critical-path attribution | Which single line gated each kit? | Procurement Manager | Wk 3 |
| Quote-to-actual variance | By configuration family; exposes padding and whether padding is doing real work | Flow Owner | Wk 3 |
| Configuration Pareto | 24 months of orders clustered by option content | Engineering Manager | Wk 4 |

**Fallback, to be started in Week 0 in parallel rather than after disappointment:** if system timestamps prove absent or unreliable — which is common, and would be nobody's fault — we proceed with (a) manual traveller stamping on the next 20 orders released, (b) a full physical value-stream walk with the three functions present together, and (c) a two-day direct observation study at each certified gate. This yields sufficient resolution in four weeks and avoids eight weeks of data archaeology.

### 3.2 Two validations before any capital is committed

- **Win/loss validation (Owner: Sales Director, with an independent interviewer; due Week 2).** 15–20 structured interviews on lost deals. This is not scepticism toward Sales; lead time is simply the most available and least uncomfortable loss reason in any organisation, and if the true driver is price, reliability or specification, the capital in this plan is misdirected. Sales' credibility is *strengthened*, not exposed, by independent confirmation.
- **Competitor reliability benchmark (Owner: Sales Director; due Week 4).** Does the competitor actually *deliver* in 6 weeks, or quote it? If they routinely miss, then a guaranteed, penalty-backed 7 weeks may be a sharper weapon than an aspirational 6 — and considerably cheaper.

---

## 4. Where the 70 working days go

**Units, stated once and used throughout: all durations in this document are *working days* at 5 per week.** 14 weeks = 70 working days; the 6-week target = 30 working days. Calendar conversions are given in brackets where relevant.

Illustrative decomposition, to be replaced by the diagnostic:

| Segment | Working days | Of which value-adding |
|---|---:|---:|
| Order entry, configuration confirmation, engineering release, contract/credit admin | 7 | 1 |
| Purchasing cycle + longest-lead item wait to kit completion | 19 | 0 |
| Fabrication / machining queue and setup wait | 8 | 3 |
| Assembly | 7 | 5 |
| Certified gate dwell (4 gates) | 7 | 1 |
| Rework and re-inspection loops (probability-weighted) | 5 | 0 |
| Final test, burn-in, certification documentation pack | 6 | 4 |
| Preservation, crating, shipping preparation | 3 | 1 |
| Quote protection buffer | 8 | 0 |
| **Total** | **70 (14 weeks)** | **15** |

## 0. Executive summary

**The situation, stated plainly and without attribution of fault.** Our revenue is lumpy because our model makes it lumpy, and the market discounts what it cannot forecast. Leadership wants recurring revenue. The modelling says we cannot get there without a multi-year trough. The field is paid on the very deals we intend to stop selling. The installed base believes — accurately — that it bought something perpetual. And the one nearby precedent we have lost a fifth of its base moving quickly.

Four constituencies each hold an internally coherent position: the field is right that its economics break; the CFO is right that the trough is real; customers are right that they own what they bought; Product is right that we cannot fund a cloud platform out of upgrade cycles. All four being right is precisely why no single function can resolve this.

**The central finding we expect the diagnostic to confirm.** The trough and the entitlement problem have almost nothing to do with each other, and are routinely confused:

- **The trough is a timing artefact of *new* business** — a licence recognised on delivery becomes an annual fee recognised ratably — compounded by the disappearance of paid-upgrade revenue.
- **Converting the installed base is revenue-*accretive*, not dilutive**, provided the subscription price sits meaningfully above current maintenance. The obstacle there is trust, not arithmetic.

The failure mode — and, we suspect, our competitor's — is **paying for the second problem with discounts that permanently deepen the first.**

**The organising principle we would propose:** *ARR list price is sacred; everything around it is fair game.* Every migration incentive must pass one test: *does this concession cost us cash once, or revenue forever?* Duration, scope, credits, terms, rights and patience are one-time currencies. # Critique — "Business-Model Transition to Subscription — First Draft for Comment"

## 1. Headline judgement

The draft has a genuinely good spine — the separation of the trough problem from the entitlement problem, and the "cost us cash once vs. revenue forever" test for incentives — and then stops before delivering any of the four things the request actually asked for. What exists is an executive summary and a set of principles. What was commissioned was an offer structure, a migration incentive ladder, a price architecture, a comp redesign, and an investor communication plan. Roughly 85% of the required content is absent, and several of the numbers in the part that does exist do not reconcile.

## 2. Fatal gap: the deliverables are not in the document

The brief named five deliverables. Coverage:

| Required | Delivered |
|---|---|
| Offer structure | A three-stage *posture* table. No SKUs, no tiers, no term-licence vs. hosted vs. on-prem-subscription decision, no multi-year prepay, no packaging of new capability |
| Migration incentives for existing licence holders | A taxonomy of currencies ("duration, scope, credits, terms, rights, patience") and nothing else. No offer ladder, no cohort targeting, no uptake assumptions, no cost-per-conversion |
| Pricing that balances trough depth against adoption | Zero prices. This is the single most consequential trade-off in the brief and it is entirely unaddressed |
| Sales compensation redesign | Two words: "comp plan shadow-run" |
| Financial communication plan | One principle ("shape, not depth") and a truncated sentence |

Worse, the preamble asserts that "the entitlement charter, the compensation mechanics, the tripwires and the decision requests are **not** placeholders and are put forward for approval." None of those four items appear anywhere in the document. Forward-referencing content that does not exist is the most damaging kind of error in a decision paper: it invites a reader to approve something they cannot see. Either write them or remove the claim.

The document also ends mid-word ("five-year cumulative rev"). It cannot be circulated in this state.

## 3. Numerical and analytical errors

**3.1 The illustrative model does not internally reconcile.** Yr 0: revenue 240, ARR 70 → ~170 of non-recurring revenue. Yr 1: ARR rises 70 → 105 (+35 exit ARR), so in-year recognised subscription revenue is roughly the average, ~85–90. For total revenue to be 205, non-recurring revenue must fall from ~170 to ~115 — a 32% collapse of perpetual **in the year the plan says perpetual remains "available, unmoved in price."** Stage 1 and the model contradict each other. Separately, "subscription mix 15%" of 205 = ~$31M, which is irreconcilable with either exit or average ARR of 105. Fix by defining exit ARR vs. average ARR, and by publishing a four-line revenue bridge (perpetual licence / paid upgrade / maintenance / subscription) for each year. An analyst will find this inconsistency in ten minutes; so will the CFO.

**3.2 "ARR $70M" in a perpetual-licence business is a terminological trap.** That figure is maintenance, not ARR. Using ARR for it inflates the starting point, understates the apparent growth of *real* subscription, and is exactly the kind of definitional looseness that costs credibility in the first analyst call after a model change. Label it "maintenance-derived recurring revenue" and report a separate, clean subscription-ARR line from day one.

**3.3 The claim that base conversion is "revenue-accretive, not dilutive" is over-confident and probably wrong as stated.** It holds for the maintenance-to-subscription substitution alone. It omits (a) the loss of that cohort's future paid-upgrade revenue, which the draft has assigned solely to the "new business" bucket, (b) the revenue impact of trade-in credits for unamortised licence value, and (c) the recognition consequences of whatever the offer actually is. The clean statement is: *conversion is accretive on recurring revenue and dilutive on total revenue for the cohorts that would have bought an upgrade in the window.* Stating it the current way will be corrected in the room, and the correction will discredit the surrounding analysis.

**3.4 A major trough-softening lever is missing entirely: term licences.** A time-based on-premise licence with no hosting obligation can, under ASC 606, be recognised substantially at delivery while still producing a renewable contract. Autodesk, PTC and others used precisely this to flatten the trough. The document does not mention it, which means the pricing/rev-rec design space has not been explored. The corollary is also missing: the trade-off between reported-revenue optics (term licence) and investor-preferred quality of revenue (SaaS, ratable). That trade-off deserves a page.

**3.5 The cash plan is a number, not a plan.** "$95M cumulative FCF shortfall … sets the liquidity requirement" is not sufficient. Required: shortfall in the downside case, not the base case; covenant headroom analysis; the financing mix (revolver, term debt, convertible); the buyback/dividend posture and the signal it sends; the effect of billings frequency (annual-in-advance vs. monthly) on the shortfall — annual prepay with a 3–5% discount is one of the largest and cheapest trough levers available and is unmentioned. Also missing: ASC 340-40 commission capitalisation, which materially changes both the P&L and the comp design.

**3.6 "Conversion ratio ≥ 2.2×" is an undefined gate.** 2.2× of maintenance? Of amortised perpetual ACV? Of prior three-year customer spend? A Stage-2 go/no-go criterion that cannot be computed unambiguously is a governance defect, not a detail.

**3.7 The competitor precedent is invoked but never diagnosed.** "Lost a fifth of its installed base" is the most useful data point in the brief and the plan does nothing with it. Required: a short forensic on *mechanism* — forced end-of-support, maintenance price coercion, mandatory move to cloud, data-migration friction, loss of offline/air-gapped capability — mapped item-by-item against what this plan does differently. Without that, the reassurance that "no customer is ever forced to move" is an assertion rather than a design.

## 4. Missing structural content

- **Installed-base segmentation.** Nothing on cohorts: maintenance-current vs. lapsed, version currency, size, vertical, renewal date, degree of customisation, air-gapped/regulated deployments. Sequencing, incentive generosity and churn risk all differ by cohort; lapsed-maintenance customers are simultaneously the largest conversion prize and the largest churn risk, and they are absent.
- **Channel and partner economics.** If any material share goes through resellers or VARs, partners are paid on upfront margin and will resist harder than the direct field. Entirely unaddressed. This is a common cause of stalled transitions.
- **Maintenance pricing stance.** Raising maintenance to narrow the gap to subscription is the classic accelerant — and the classic cause of the very base revolt the brief warns about. The plan must take an explicit position rather than leave it silent.
- **Tripwires and abort criteria.** Referenced, never specified. Needs numbers: conversion-cohort gross logo churn, net dollar retention, new-logo subscription win rate, field attrition, cash floor — each with a named owner and a defined consequence (decelerate Stage 2, extend perpetual availability, increase incentive spend).
- **People risk.** Field attrition during comp transition, and employee equity value during a depressed share price, are both first-order execution risks. Neither appears.
- **Auditor and Audit Committee workstream.** A rev-rec change of this scale needs a pre-cleared technical position before anything is announced.
- **Units and timeline discipline.** The document mixes "Week 8", "Q1–Q2", "Yr 2" and "Yr 3+" without a stated convention — a lapse the antecedent document specifically made a virtue of avoiding.

## 5. Framing and governance problems

- **Audience is wrong for a working draft.** Placing the Audit Committee chair and lead independent director "in attendance" at a management alignment session risks pre-committing directors to management's framing before management itself has aligned. Sequence it: management alignment → CFO/Audit Committee technical review → full board education session with the model.
- **The hedging is mis-calibrated to the decision state.** Leadership has already decided to move to subscription. Hedging every recommendation ("we would propose", "it may be worth agreeing") on the *path* reads as indecision on a settled question. Reserve the hedges for the numbers, which genuinely are provisional, and be flatly directive on architecture, comp and disclosure.
- **"Without attribution of fault"** is transplanted from a different problem. No one is at fault here; the phrase imports a defensiveness the situation does not carry and slightly implies otherwise.
- **Unlabelled assumption.** "Product is right that we cannot fund a cloud platform out of upgrade cycles" introduces a cloud re-platforming programme that the brief never mentions. If a platform rebuild is in scope, it changes the cost, the timeline and the customer-migration difficulty enormously and must be stated as a premise up front, with its own cost line.
- **Style is derivative to the point of distraction.** The sacred/fair-game device, the "four constituencies each internally coherent" construction, the illustrative-placeholder preamble and the staged commitment table are lifted wholesale from the lead-time document. Some transfer well (the one-time-vs-permanent-currency test is excellent and original in application). Others are ceremony that displaces the substance the reader actually needs.
- **Grammar.** "the one nearby precedent we have lost a fifth of its base moving quickly" is garbled.

## 6. What a passing version must contain

1. **Offer architecture table**: subscription tiers; term-licence vs. hosted vs. on-prem subscription; what new capability is subscription-only and from when; multi-year and prepay options; the explicit fallback offer for customers who genuinely cannot move (regulated, air-gapped).
2. **Entitlement charter**, one page, customer-facing language: perpetual licences remain valid in perpetuity; no forced end-of-support inside N years; dual-run rights during conversion; data portability and exit guarantee.
3. **Migration incentive ladder**, as a table with each item classified *cash-once* or *revenue-forever*, priced, with target cohort and assumed uptake: trade-in credit for unamortised licence, 3-year price lock, free migration services, extra seats/modules for a fixed term, first-year ramp pricing, retained perpetual as fallback. Total incentive budget and the cap per cohort.
4. **Price architecture with numbers and two sensitivities**: subscription at (say) 28% vs. 35% of perpetual list, showing the effect of each on trough depth, breakeven year, conversion rate and five-year cumulative revenue. This is the balance the brief asked for and it must be shown as a trade-off, not a point estimate.
5. **Comp redesign**: ACV-based quota with multi-year multipliers; explicit conversion accelerator; renewal/expansion credit split; a two-year quota-relief and earnings-floor guarantee to hold the field; clawbacks; treatment of ramping reps; a published schedule for retiring perpetual bookings credit; and the partner-margin analogue. Include a worked example for a representative rep, before and after — nothing persuades a CRO faster.
6. **Financial communication plan**: metric change-over (subscription ARR, RPO, billings, NDR, cohort conversion), the pre-announced trough curve with named quarterly waypoints, guidance philosophy (multi-year framework, not quarterly precision), the analyst-day sequencing relative to results, the pre-agreed script for the first waypoint miss, comparable-company framing, and the board-level dashboard with tripwires.
7. **Reconciled model**: four-line revenue bridge per year, downside case, liquidity requirement with buffer and financing mix.
8. **Risk register with owners and abort criteria.**

## 7. Two things worth preserving

- The trough/entitlement separation, and the diagnosis that the failure mode is "paying for the second problem with discounts that permanently deepen the first." That is the sharpest idea in the draft and should open the final version.
- "We will be judged on the shape of the trough we predicted, more than the depth of the trough we hit." Correct, and it should drive the entire disclosure design rather than sit as a stray aphorism.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
[END QUALITY FEEDBACK]

- **Maintenance pricing stance.** Raising maintenance to narrow the gap to subscription is the classic accelerant — and the classic cause of the very base revolt the brief warns about. The plan must take an explicit position rather than leave it silent.
- **Tripwires and abort criteria.** Referenced, never specified. Needs numbers: conversion-cohort gross logo churn, net dollar retention, new-logo subscription win rate, field attrition, cash floor — each with a named owner and a defined consequence (decelerate Stage 2, extend perpetual availability, increase incentive spend).
- **People risk.** Field attrition during comp transition, and employee equity value during a depressed share price, are both first-order execution risks. Neither appears.
- **Auditor and Audit Committee workstream.** A rev-rec change of this scale needs a pre-cleared technical position before anything is announced.
- **Units and timeline discipline.** The document mixes "Week 8", "Q1–Q2", "Yr 2" and "Yr 3+" without a stated convention — a lapse the antecedent document specifically made a virtue of avoiding.

## 5. Framing and governance problems

- **Audience is wrong for a working draft.** Placing the Audit Committee chair and lead independent director "in attendance" at a management alignment session risks pre-committing directors to management's framing before management itself has aligned. Sequence it: management alignment → CFO/Audit Committee technical review → full board education session with the model.
- **The hedging is mis-calibrated to the decision state.** Leadership has already decided to move to subscription. Hedging every recommendation ("we would propose", "it may be worth agreeing") on the *path* reads as indecision on a settled question. Reserve the hedges for the numbers, which genuinely are provisional, and be flatly directive on architecture, comp and disclosure.
- **"Without attribution of fault"** is transplanted from a different problem. No one is at fault here; the phrase imports a defensiveness the situation does not carry and slightly implies otherwise.
- **Unlabelled assumption.** "Product is right that we cannot fund a cloud platform out of upgrade cycles" introduces a cloud re-platforming programme that the brief never mentions. If a platform rebuild is in scope, it changes the cost, the timeline and the customer-migration difficulty enormously and must be stated as a premise up front, with its own cost line.
- **Style is derivative to the point of distraction.** The sacred/fair-game device, the "four constituencies each internally coherent" construction, the illustrative-placeholder preamble and the staged commitment table are lifted wholesale from the lead-time document. Some transfer well (the one-time-vs-permanent-currency test is excellent and original in application). Others are ceremony that displaces the substance the reader actually needs.
- **Grammar.** "the one nearby precedent we have lost a fifth of its base moving quickly" is garbled.

## 6. What a passing version must contain

1. **Offer architecture table**: subscription tiers; term-licence vs. hosted vs. on-prem subscription; what new capability is subscription-only and from when; multi-year and prepay options; the explicit fallback offer for customers who genuinely cannot move (regulated, air-gapped).
2. **Entitlement charter**, one page, customer-facing language: perpetual licences remain valid in perpetuity; no forced end-of-support inside N years; dual-run rights during conversion; data portability and exit guarantee.
3. **Migration incentive ladder**, as a table with each item classified *cash-once* or *revenue-forever*, priced, with target cohort and assumed uptake: trade-in credit for unamortised licence, 3-year price lock, free migration services, extra seats/modules for a fixed term, first-year ramp pricing, retained perpetual as fallback. Total incentive budget and the cap per cohort.
4. **Price architecture with numbers and two sensitivities**: subscription at (say) 28% vs. 35% of perpetual list, showing the effect of each on trough depth, breakeven year, conversion rate and five-year cumulative revenue. This is the balance the brief asked for and it must be shown as a trade-off, not a point estimate.
5. **Comp redesign**: ACV-based quota with multi-year multipliers; explicit conversion accelerator; renewal/expansion credit split; a two-year quota-relief and earnings-floor guarantee to hold the field; clawbacks; treatment of ramping reps; a published schedule for retiring perpetual bookings credit; and the partner-margin analogue. Include a worked example for a representative rep, before and after — nothing persuades a CRO faster.
6. **Financial communication plan**: metric change-over (subscription ARR, RPO, billings, NDR, cohort conversion), the pre-announced trough curve with named quarterly waypoints, guidance philosophy (multi-year framework, not quarterly precision), the analyst-day sequencing relative to results, the pre-agreed script for the first waypoint miss, comparable-company framing, and the board-level dashboard with tripwires.
7. **Reconciled model**: four-line revenue bridge per year, downside case, liquidity requirement with buffer and financing mix.
8. **Risk register with owners and abort criteria.**

## 7. Two things worth preserving

- The trough/entitlement separation, and the diagnosis that the failure mode is "paying for the second problem with discounts that permanently deepen the first." That is the sharpest idea in the draft and should open the final version.
- "We will be judged on the shape of the trough we predicted, more than the depth of the trough we hit." Correct, and it should drive the entire disclosure design rather than sit as a stray aphorism.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
